summary: Summarizes OAM tools defined in the IETF for IP unicast, MPLS, MPLS-TP, pseudowires, and TRILL. The focus is on detecting and isolating failures and on performance monitoring. It can serve as an index to the main OAM tools.

plainLanguage.summary: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) tools help check whether a network path works, locate failures, and measure performance. This RFC is a guide to IETF tools for several network technologies.

questions: overview of oam in mpls and ip
how do you detect network failures
subtitle: An index to IETF tools for checking connectivity, tracing paths, and measuring network performance.

tldr.problem: Network operators need ways to detect and locate failures and measure performance across different network technologies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys IETF Operations, Administration, and Maintenance tools for IP, BFD, MPLS, MPLS-TP, pseudowires, OWAMP, TWAMP, and TRILL.
tldr.outcome: This Informational document is an index and overview of data-plane monitoring tools. It does not specify network repair functions or control and management procedures.

today: RFC 7276 is an Informational overview published in June 2014. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it serves as an index to the IETF OAM tools described in the RFC.

sections.title: What OAM Covers
sections.content:
Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) is a set of tools for detecting and isolating failures and measuring network performance. RFC 7276 surveys IETF tools for IP unicast, Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS), MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP), pseudowires, and Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL).

The document focuses on tools that monitor the data plane, where packets are forwarded. It does not cover control and management functions or network repair methods such as fast reroute and protection switching.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM tools test the path that carries network traffic. This RFC collects examples for several technologies but does not describe how a network repairs a failure.

sections.title: OAM Functions and Activation
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes an OAM function, which is a measurement or diagnostic capability, from a protocol that implements functions and a tool that applies them. Common functions include continuity checks, connectivity verification, path discovery, fault localization, packet-loss measurement, and delay measurement.

Tools may run proactively, sending messages regularly and reporting when expected messages stop, or on demand when an operator investigates a particular issue. Continuity checks test reachability; connectivity verification can also check whether traffic follows an expected path. The document emphasizes that monitoring packets should share the treatment of the traffic they measure.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM can check reachability, verify a path, locate a fault, or measure loss and delay. A tool can run continuously or only when someone requests a check.

sections.title: IP, BFD, and MPLS Tools
sections.content:
IP Ping sends an ICMP Echo request and waits for a reply, testing reachability from the requesting side. IP Traceroute sends probes with increasing Time to Live values; routers return messages that reveal hops along a path. Traceroute finds a path, but IP routing may be asymmetric, so it does not reveal the reverse path.

Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is a generic tool that can run over several encapsulations. It can send control packets periodically or on demand and declares a session down after the negotiated detection period passes without expected packets. MPLS LSP Ping checks connectivity along a label-switched path, while its traceroute mode helps locate a fault hop by hop.
sections.plainLanguage: Ping asks whether a destination responds, while traceroute shows the routers along one path. BFD checks a session for missing control messages, and LSP Ping applies similar checks to an MPLS path.

sections.title: Transport and Performance Tools
sections.content:
MPLS-TP OAM includes continuity and connectivity checks, route tracing, lock and alarm functions, remote defect indication, and performance measurement. Pseudowire OAM uses a control channel such as VCCV to carry tools including ICMP Ping, LSP Ping, and BFD. The RFC also summarizes tools for TRILL.

The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) measures one-way IP performance and requires accurate time at its endpoints. The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) supports one-way and round-trip measurements. Their test packets can measure loss, delay, duplication, and reordering; the RFC notes that measurement accuracy depends on implementation and network configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Different network technologies use different OAM methods, including special checks for MPLS-TP and pseudowires. OWAMP and TWAMP send test packets to measure network performance.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attack on OAM can create a false report of failure or hide a real failure, potentially causing denial of service. Some tools provide integrity protection or authentication, and OWAMP and TWAMP define unauthenticated, authenticated, and encrypted modes.

OAM can also reveal addresses, port numbers, topology, and performance. Operators and implementors need to consider both forged monitoring messages and information gathered through valid probes.
sections.plainLanguage: False OAM messages can mislead operators, while real probes can reveal network details. Some tools support authentication or encryption, but their security features differ.
